awd_abstract_narration:
2520357 (Flach). This workshop will examine the current and future marketplace of industrial bioprocessing feedstocks. It will gather researchers and practitioners with a variety of skillsets, from systems-level modeling to metabolic engineering and bioprocess experts, facilitating an environment for cross-field interactions. The two key aims will be to answer the following questions: (1) What new, sustainable feedstocks have an opportunity to be more effectively incorporated into the circular bioeconomy? (2) What has been learned about the commercialization viability of past feedstocks, and how can those lessons be applied to ongoing efforts? The workshop will take place over a full day and has two primary objectives: (1) Converge a community with a wide array of expertise areas to learn from the experiences of past leaders, applying those lessons to current initiatives; (2) Facilitate a focused discussion among experts to identify strategies for moving forward and the challenges that must be addressed to advance the circular bioeconomy. Following these discussions, a report will be issued, summarizing takeaways from key case studies and offering a path forward on how to most effectively address challenges related to industrial bioprocessing feedstocks to advance the circular bioeconomy. The workshop presents a unique opportunity to gain insights from leaders in industry, academia, and government, each bringing a wide range of expertise. It is targeted to be held in November at the 2025 AIChE Annual Meeting at the Hynes Convention Center in Boston, Massachusetts. 

This workshop program will involve experts in the field sharing their insights with the next generation dedicated to advancing the circular bioeconomy. It will bring together current leaders to discuss the challenges and achievements present in today’s circular bioeconomy landscape. Following the workshop, a report will be issued that summarizes presentations, discussions, and findings. The report will highlight current challenges and where to invest resources to overcome them. It will be publicly available and distributed through AIChE’s website, helping others in the community learn from the event. Facilitating knowledge transfer from long-experienced experts to the future generation of engineers advancing the circular bioeconomy will have long term impacts on the development of the circular bioeconomy. Sharing lessons learned and past mistakes will help current engineers and researchers avoid the same pitfalls.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported the 2025 Circular Bioeconomy Workshop, held on November 2, 2025, in Boston, Massachusetts, alongside the AIChE Annual Meeting. The workshop brought together leaders from academia, industry, and government to examine a major challenge facing the circular bioeconomy: how to develop reliable, scalable, and sustainable industrial bioprocessing feedstocks. The event included expert presentations, case studies, and a focused roundtable discussion designed to capture lessons from past bioeconomy commercialization efforts and identify practical strategies for future progress.

The project advanced intellectual merit by clarifying the technical and systems-level barriers that limit the use of biomass, waste streams, and other circular resources as industrial feedstocks. Participants emphasized that feedstock reliability is often as important as conversion technology itself. Variability in biomass composition, moisture, ash content, particle size, morphology, contaminants, and seasonal availability can disrupt preprocessing, fermentation, thermochemical conversion, and downstream operations. The workshop highlighted that many past commercialization challenges were caused not only by conversion chemistry, but also by inconsistent feedstock quality, weak supply chains, poor solids handling, and insufficient understanding of real-world variability.

A major outcome of the workshop was the identification of feedstock reliability engineering as a high-priority research and deployment need. Participants recommended developing common feedstock quality specifications, including standardized measures for organic or convertible carbon, moisture, ash, particle size, and contaminants. They identified preprocessing, densification, blending, and improved solids-handling technologies as near-term tools for reducing operational risk. The workshop further emphasized the need for integrated techno-economic analysis and sustainability assessment early in technology development, so that feedstock cost, logistics, environmental performance, and market fit are evaluated together rather than separately.

The project identified important future research directions. These include developing shared, machine-readable feedstock characterization databases; launching regional feedstock reliability pilots; improving models that account for variability in real supply chains; and creating contaminant screening and mitigation strategies for circular feedstocks such as municipal waste, agricultural residues, and wastewater-derived materials. Participants stressed that regional context matters: the most effective feedstock strategy will depend on local crop availability, logistics infrastructure, land use, market demand, and environmental goals.

The award produced broader impacts by creating a forum for knowledge transfer across generations, sectors, and disciplines. Experienced leaders shared lessons from past biofuel and bioproduct efforts with current researchers, engineers, trainees, and early-career professionals. The workshop helped participants understand why some previous deployment efforts struggled and how future projects can better align technology readiness, feedstock availability, market needs, and sustainability goals. The event strengthened connections among communities working on systems modeling, metabolic engineering, bioprocessing, biomass logistics, sustainability, and commercialization.

The workshop outcomes will inform the broader circular bioeconomy community through a written report summarizing presentations, discussion themes, findings, and recommended next steps. By making these lessons available through AIChE and its Society for Biological Engineering, the project extends beyond the participants who attended the event and supports a wider community of researchers, companies, students, and decision-makers working to build a more resilient, sustainable, and economically viable bioeconomy.
